title: Ezekiel 11:14–25
context: The LORD answers Ezekiel’s cry. Jerusalem’s inhabitants had told the exiles to go far from the LORD and claimed the land for themselves, but the LORD promises to be a sanctuary for the scattered for a little while, to gather them, and to give them the land. He will give them one heart and a new spirit, replacing the stony heart with a heart of flesh so that they walk in his ways, while those devoted to idols will bear their own way. Related promises appear at Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:26–27, each in its own setting. The glory of the LORD then leaves the city and stands on the mountain to the east, and Ezekiel is brought back in the vision to the exiles in Chaldea and tells them all he has seen.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s word comes to Ezekiel. A new message begins, answering the prophet’s cry about the remnant.

Arminian readers see God responding to his servant’s anguish with a word of hope, not silence.
verses.reformedNotes:
The answer follows directly on the question of 11:13 about a full end of the remnant.

Reformed readers see God answering in his own way and time. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God hearing his servant’s cry.

verses.text: “Son of man, your brothers, even your brothers, the men of your relatives, and all the house of Israel, all of them, are the ones to whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem have said, ‘Go far away from the LORD. This land has been given to us for a possession.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says that Jerusalem’s inhabitants told the exiles, Ezekiel’s own relatives, “Go far away from the LORD. This land has been given to us for a possession.” Those left behind claim the land.

Arminian readers see presumption in that claim.
verses.reformedNotes:
Those still in Jerusalem seem to have treated the exiles as cut off from God.

Reformed readers see God rejecting claims based on mere location. Both traditions read this as shared ground about presuming on privilege.

verses.text: “Therefore say, ‘The Lord GOD says: “Whereas I have removed them far off among the nations, and whereas I have scattered them among the countries, yet I will be to them a sanctuary for a little while in the countries where they have come.” ’
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord GOD says that although he scattered them among the nations, he will be to them “a sanctuary for a little while” in the countries where they have gone. God is present in exile.

Arminian readers see grace reaching the scattered.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase may mean a sanctuary in small measure or for a limited time; both readings are offered.

Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness outside the land. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s presence with his people far from the temple.

verses.text: “Therefore say, ‘The Lord GOD says: “I will gather you from the peoples, and assemble you out of the countries where you have been scattered, and I will give you the land of Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord GOD promises to gather them from the peoples and give them the land of Israel. The exiles, not those who claimed the land, receive the promise.

Arminian readers see God’s gracious restoration offered to the scattered people.
verses.reformedNotes:
The promise reverses the claim in verse 15.

Reformed readers see God’s purpose to restore his people. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s faithfulness to gather his people, and readers differ on how far the promise extends beyond the return from exile.

verses.text: “ ‘They will come there, and they will take away all its detestable things and all its abominations from there.
verses.arminianNotes:
When they return, they will remove all the detestable things and abominations from the land. Restoration involves cleansing.

Arminian readers see the returning people actively turning from idolatry.
verses.reformedNotes:
The removal of idols anticipates the inward change promised in the next verse.

Reformed readers see renewal producing visible purification. Both traditions read this as shared ground about restoration bringing a real break with idolatry, which chapter 8 had described in the temple itself.

verses.text: I will give them one heart, and I will put a new spirit within them. I will take the stony heart out of their flesh, and will give them a heart of flesh,
verses.arminianNotes:
“I will give them one heart, and I will put a new spirit within them.” Arminian readers see grace renewing the heart and enabling a response.

The boxes at Deuteronomy 5:29 and 10:16 treat this; see also Deuteronomy 30:6. They set out how this tradition relates grace and response.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God giving the heart that makes obedience sure, replacing “the stony heart” with “a heart of flesh.”

Related promises appear at Jeremiah 31:33 (compare Hebrews 8:10) and Ezekiel 36:26–27, each in its own setting. Both traditions read the promise as God’s gracious work.

verses.text: that they may walk in my statutes, and keep my ordinances, and do them. They will be my people, and I will be their God.
verses.arminianNotes:
The new heart is given so that they may walk in God’s statutes and keep his ordinances. Arminian readers see obedience flowing from renewal and continued by faith.

The covenant formula follows: “They will be my people, and I will be their God.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see obedience as the certain fruit of the new heart.

The same formula appears at Jeremiah 31:33 and 24:7. Both traditions read the verse as joining inward renewal and outward obedience, without opening a new divide here.

verses.text: But as for them whose heart walks after the heart of their detestable things and their abominations, I will bring their way on their own heads,’ says the Lord GOD.”
verses.arminianNotes:
But those whose heart follows their detestable things will have their way brought on their own heads. A warning accompanies the promise.

Arminian readers see the promise of renewal set beside personal accountability.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse makes clear that the promise does not cancel responsibility.

Reformed readers see judgment on those who remain in idolatry. Both traditions read this as shared ground: God’s promise of a new heart and his warning against persistent idolatry stand side by side.

verses.text: Then the cherubim lifted up their wings, and the wheels were beside them. The glory of the God of Israel was over them above.
verses.arminianNotes:
The cherubim lift their wings, with the wheels beside them, and the glory of the God of Israel is above them. The vision resumes.

Arminian readers see the solemn movement of God’s presence away from the place that had rejected him.
verses.reformedNotes:
The description recalls 10:19, where the cherubim stood at the east gate.

Reformed readers see God’s glory as his to give or withdraw. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the seriousness of sin that drives away the sense of God’s presence.

verses.text: The LORD’s glory went up from the middle of the city, and stood on the mountain which is on the east side of the city.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD’s glory rises from the city and stands on the mountain east of it. The glory departs.

Arminian readers see God withdrawing in judgment, though not abandoning his purposes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Many identify the mountain with the Mount of Olives, though the text does not name it. In 43:2 the glory returns “from the way of the east.”

Reformed readers see departure followed by promised return. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: The Spirit lifted me up, and brought me in the vision by the Spirit of God into Chaldea, to the captives. So the vision that I had seen went up from me.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Spirit lifts Ezekiel and brings him in the vision to Chaldea, to the captives, and the vision leaves him. The visionary journey ends.

Arminian readers see the prophet returned to his people to share what he has seen.
verses.reformedNotes:
The vision that began in 8:1–3 now closes, with Ezekiel back among the exiles.

Reformed readers see the Spirit guiding the prophet. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the Spirit’s role in prophecy and the exiles as recipients of the message.

verses.text: Then I spoke to the captives all the things that the LORD had shown me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ezekiel tells the captives everything the LORD has shown him. The message is passed on.

Arminian readers see the exiles given the full account so they can understand and respond, despite Jerusalem’s claims against them.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse completes the frame of the vision begun in chapter 8.

Reformed readers see faithful witness to God’s revelation. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the prophet’s duty to report fully and the exiles’ privilege of hearing God’s word.
